summaries.example: Imagine following a trail of spilled cereal in a store. You think, “That shopper made the mess.” Then you notice the trail comes from your own cart. You already knew someone made the mess, but you did not yet realize that the shopper was you. That new thought changes what you do.
summaries.summary: A self-locating belief is a thought about your own place or situation in the world. You might know that a meeting starts at noon but not notice that it is noon right now. You might know that a person is making a mess but not realize that the person is you. These cases suggest that knowing ordinary facts is not always enough to explain what people know, how they change their minds, or why they act. Philosophers study whether self-locating beliefs form a special kind of belief. Some, including David Lewis, describe them using possibilities that include a world and a particular person or time within it. Others, including John Perry, focus on the mental method or “belief state” through which a person thinks. The same issue also affects how people communicate and how they update beliefs over time.
key_ideas: A person can know many facts and still not know that those facts describe them.
Words like “I,” “here,” and “now” point from a person’s situation.
Self-locating beliefs can explain why two people who know the same facts act differently.
Philosophers disagree about whether the special feature is the content of a belief or the way a person holds it.
summaries.why_it_matters: This idea helps explain everyday moments of realization. It also asks an important question about knowledge: Is knowing how the world is enough, or must we also know how we fit into it? The question connects thinking, language, communication, and decision-making.

important_terms.definition: A belief about where you are, who you are, what time it is for you, or what situation you are in.
A word such as “I,” “here,” or “now” whose meaning depends on the situation in which it is used.
A person’s mental state of believing, not just what they know about the world but how they understand their own place in it.
Not knowing something about yourself or your own situation, even when you know many facts about the world.

questions_to_think_about: Can you know that someone is late without realizing that you are the late person?
When does the word “here” change what a sentence means?
If two people know the same facts, why might they still behave differently?
Is knowing “I am the one affected” different from knowing that someone is affected?

summaries.example: Suppose a professor believes throughout the morning that a meeting begins at noon. Before noon, that belief does not move him to leave. At the relevant moment, he comes to believe, in a first-personal way, that the meeting begins now, and he starts walking. The ordinary fact may have stayed the same, while his self-locating state changed.
summaries.summary: Self-locating beliefs are beliefs about one’s own position or situation, broadly construed. The motivating cases suggest that a subject may possess all the relevant ordinary descriptive or de re beliefs and still lack a first-personal understanding that matters for knowledge, cognition, or action. Perry’s messy-shopper case illustrates this: the subject believes that a particular shopper is making a mess, yet only later realizes that he is that shopper. Related arguments concern differences in behavior between agents who share the same ordinary beliefs, and similarities between agents whose corresponding first-person thoughts are true for one and false for another. These arguments challenge a “Simple Picture” on which belief is merely a relation between a person and traditional, world-directed propositions. Lewis proposes centered worlds or centered propositions, which represent a world together with a time and individual. Perry instead emphasizes belief states, understood as context-sensitive mechanisms that can connect different people in corresponding ways to different propositions. The broader debate extends to immunity to error through misidentification, communication, and Bayesian updating. In communication, a speaker’s self-locating state cannot always simply be transferred unchanged to an addressee; proposals include recentering, decentering, and restricting which states are communicable. In updating, standard conditionalization struggles with self-locating claims whose truth changes as the agent’s temporal position changes. The entry also considers objections that these cases may be ordinary Frege-style cases or that action can be explained without self-locating beliefs.
key_ideas: The central cases involve ignorance, change, and similarity or difference that ordinary descriptive and de re beliefs seem unable to capture.
In the messy-shopper case, a person already believes that a certain individual is making a mess but lacks the self-locating realization that he himself is that individual.
Lewis responds by enriching the objects of belief: centered propositions distinguish positions within worlds.
Perry responds by enriching the belief relation: belief states track context-sensitive mechanisms by which a person is related to propositions.
The issue is not limited to geographic location; it can concern identity, time, properties, abilities, or a person’s role in a situation.
Self-locating beliefs create further problems for communication and formal updating, and the best solution remains disputed.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic tests what a theory of mind must represent in order to explain knowledge, belief revision, action, and interpersonal communication. It also shows why a sentence can preserve ordinary factual information while changing its practical significance when expressed with “I,” “here,” or “now.” The debate illustrates how philosophy separates a phenomenon from competing models of that phenomenon.

important_terms.definition: A belief concerning the believer’s own position, identity, time, or situation within reality, broadly understood rather than merely as a geographic location.
An expression whose reference varies with context, such as “I,” “here,” or “now.”
A proposition that determines truth relative only to how the world is, not to a more specific person, time, or standpoint within that world.
A centered possibility represented roughly as a world together with a time and an individual located within it.
A first-personal attitude concerning oneself as oneself; Lewis uses “de se” for this kind of attitude.
A cognitive condition characterized partly by the mechanism or representational pattern through which a person becomes related to a proposition.
An error in which someone correctly identifies a feature but mistakes whose feature it is; some first-person judgments may avoid this kind of error.
A rule for changing degrees of belief in response to information; standard Bayesian conditionalization has difficulty with self-locating contents whose truth changes as time passes.

questions_to_think_about: Does the difference between “John is being attacked” and “I am being attacked” concern content, belief state, or both?
Can two people share a self-locating belief-state while believing different traditional propositions?
Why might sending a speaker’s “my pants are on fire” state directly to a listener produce a false belief?
Can a theory explain action differences without self-locating representations by appealing instead to abilities?
How should a belief-update rule handle a proposition that is false before noon but true at noon?

summaries.example: You know that the school bell rings at 3:00 and that a student who misses it will be late. At 3:00, you are still sitting in class because you have not connected the fact “the bell is ringing at 3:00” with “it is ringing now, and I need to leave.” Your information about the schedule stayed similar, but your understanding of your own situation changed.
summaries.summary: A self-locating belief concerns one’s own place in a situation: who one is, where one is, when something is happening, or which role one occupies. The idea is motivated by cases in which ordinary knowledge does not explain a person’s ignorance or behavior. In the supermarket example, someone believes that a particular shopper is making a mess, yet fails to realize that the shopper is himself. His later first-personal realization changes his conduct even though the relevant descriptive fact was already accepted. Other arguments compare two people who share the same ordinary beliefs but behave differently, or two people who share a first-personal pattern of thought even though one person’s thought is true and the other’s is false. These cases challenge the Simple Picture, which treats belief as a relation to traditional propositions that describe whole possible worlds. Lewis’s approach adds centered worlds: possibilities include a world plus a particular person and time. Perry’s approach keeps traditional propositions but adds belief states, or context-sensitive ways of being related to them. The debate also concerns whether some first-person judgments are immune to error through misidentification. In philosophy of language, self-locating communication does not always work like passing an identical “package” of belief from speaker to listener. In formal epistemology, ordinary Bayesian updating rules may fail when a self-locating proposition changes truth as time passes. The entry presents these arguments and proposals without treating one solution as settled.
key_ideas: Self-locating ignorance can remain even after a person learns many ordinary facts about the world.
Arguments from difference focus on people who share ordinary beliefs but respond differently because they occupy different perspectives or situations.
Arguments from sameness focus on people who share a first-personal pattern of thought even when the truth of their thoughts differs.
Lewis and Perry agree that the Simple Picture faces difficulties, but they locate the needed extra structure in different places.
Self-location includes temporal and practical position, not only knowing where one is on a map.
The same questions affect language, communication, and how beliefs are updated.
summaries.why_it_matters: Self-location matters because people do not merely store facts; they use information from a particular perspective. A theory that ignores this may miss why a realization changes behavior, why communication must sometimes shift a speaker’s perspective for a listener, or why updating rules struggle with time-sensitive first-person claims.

important_terms.definition: A belief about the believer’s own identity, location, time, or role in a situation, understood more broadly than a map location.
A context-dependent word or phrase, such as “I,” “now,” or “here.”
A belief about a particular person or object, rather than merely a general description.
A description-based belief, such as believing that the person carrying the torn bag is making a mess.
A person’s way of representing something, including the context-sensitive method that connects thought with action.
A model in which belief is mainly a relation between a person and propositions that describe how a whole possible world is.
A possible world considered together with a particular person and time within that world.
A first-personal belief about oneself as oneself; “de se” is a technical term often used for this idea.

questions_to_think_about: Why does learning “that person is making a mess” seem different from learning “I am making a mess”?
Could two people have the same ordinary beliefs but different self-locating beliefs?
Would telling someone “you are the person we are looking for” give them a new fact, a new belief state, or both?
Why is a belief about “now” harder to update than a belief about a fixed historical fact?
Which seems more promising: changing what beliefs are about or changing how people are related to beliefs?
